title: Why Import
goal: This lesson covers why Python lets you import ready-made toolboxes called modules.
learn: Modules are toolboxes of useful code
Import unlocks tools you did not write
You still write the rest of the program
idea: Python comes with ready-made toolboxes called modules. Instead of inventing square roots or dice from scratch, you import a module and use its tools. Imports keep your programs shorter, and they let you build on tools that other people, and Python itself, already made.

lines: print("Then you call the tools you need")
output: Then you call the tools you need

changeOneLine: In the editor above, change the last line to mention math or random and press Run.

practice.text: Print two reasons imports are useful.
practice.hint: You need two print() lines. Each one should say something helpful about imports, like saving time or using ready-made tools.
practice.starterTip: Try print("Imports give you tools you did not write") and print("They keep programs shorter").
practice.gradingNote: Pass if two non-empty prints about modules/tools/imports.

practice.text: Print the names of two modules you will learn: math and random.
practice.hint: Use two print() calls, one for math and one for random. Put each name inside quotes.
practice.starterTip: For example: print("math") on the first line and print("random") on the second.
practice.gradingNote: Pass if math and random both appear in output.

quiz.question: What is a module?

options.text: A toolbox of useful ready-made code

quiz.correct: Right, a module bundles tools you can import.

quiz.question: Why import?

options.text: To use tools without rewriting them

quiz.correct: Yes, reusing tools beats reinventing them.

quiz.question: After you import, who writes the rest of the program?
quiz.correct: Right, modules help but you still design the program.
quiz.wrong: You are the one calling the tools.
